title: Offcut
pitch: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet.
about_excerpt: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet. Like Comment Story Updates fresh-human-review human-review planning-tradeoffs Cutting layout Inspiration A cutting plan is not just an answer—it is a decision about real material. For small workshops and makerspaces, planning starts with measured boards, usable offcuts, required parts, and the material lost to the saw blade. Copying that information into a chatbot creates a second version of the workshop: someone must reconcile the advice with the actual stock and translate it back into a usable cut sheet. Offcut explores a different workflow: let the person and the browser agent work from the same committed measurements, while keeping proposal and approval separate. Cutting-stock optimization is established work. Our contribution is the shared human–agent workflow around it: structured comparison, an exact review handoff, and approval that becomes invalid when its underlying measurements change. What it does Offcut is a shared cutting-stock workbench for straight crosscuts from stock of the same material and cross-section. People can: Enter stock lengths and required part quantities. Set blade kerf and the minimum length considered reusable. Protect stock needed for another job. Compare proportional cutting layouts. Review and approve an exact plan. Export its CSV cut list or print its cut sheet. Through native WebMCP tools, a browser agent can read the committed workshop, request checked alternatives, inspect their constraints, compare results, and stage one complete proposal for review. Three objectives make the trade-offs explicit: Use less stock Handle fewer boards Keep useful offcuts Sawdust, short scrap, reusable remnants, and unopened stock remain separate. A plan that produces less short scrap can still open more stock and require handling more boards; Offcut shows that trade-off instead of hiding it behind a single “waste” score. How we built it Offcut is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vite and published on GitHub Pages , with public MIT-licensed source. The interface and agent tools use the same workshop store and deterministic branch-and-bound planner. The language model chooses what to explore; the application checks part quantities, stock constraints, and material balance. Six JSON-schema-defined tools are registered through the browser’s native WebMCP API: get_workshop plan_cuts inspect_plan compare_plans stage_plan_for_review export_cut_list There is no WebMCP polyfill, embedded chatbot, application backend, or website API key. Manual planning also works without WebMCP. Connecting an agent depends on the browser host’s own model, permissions, and availability. The planner works in integer millimetres and has a bounded search. It reports optimality only when proved—not simply because it found a complete plan. Challenges we faced Keeping approval attached to the right decision Selecting another draft must not transfer approval. Reusing a checked solution must not transfer approval either. Approval belongs to one exact plan ID at one committed workshop revision. Acknowledgement and approval are separate interface actions; neither is a registered agent tool. Export checks the exact approved, fresh, complete plan. This is a tool-capability boundary, not authentication against an agent separately granted browser UI control. Distinguishing unfinished typing from changed measurements An unfinished measurement field is not a new workshop revision. Offcut distinguishes pending edits from saved measurements. Pending edits pause review and approval. Committing an actual change invalidates the previous approval and makes the old plan stale, so the agent must replan and return for a new review. Making native integration verifiable We tested real native tool registration, discovery, calls, disposal, and reinitialization across Chrome 149 and 152, including their differing API behavior. The demo uses a real model through an external recording harness. Its evidence rail summarizes retained native calls and UI events; it is not an embedded website chatbot or a ChatGPT screen recording. UI actions are automated for the recording, and waiting time is trimmed. Preserving correctness while improving performance We improved search pruning, reused checked solutions for identical committed requests, and reduced repeated UI work. Reuse still creates a new unapproved plan record and preserves the original computation’s proof status. What we learned Shared state matters more than conversational fluency. An agent becomes more useful when it can work with the same revision, identities, and constraints that the person sees. Approval is a state transition, not a reassuring message. Its meaning depends on the exact proposal, the measurements behind it, and what happens when those measurements change. Optimization needs explainable trade-offs. Less scrap, fewer boards, and less opened stock are different goals. The application should expose those differences rather than pretend one score answers every workshop’s priorities. Native tools should expose checked domain operations. The model can explore and explain alternatives without inventing measurements or bypassing the workbench’s release rules. What we accomplished Offcut 1.1.0 passed 884 source-contract tests and 72 browser cases : 18 contracts across local and hosted deployments in Chrome 149 and 152. We also verified the maximum 40-cut CSV export and visually checked all 12 rendered pages across two six-page print outputs. The 2:45 demo follows a complete workflow: compare alternatives, stage a proposal, acknowledge and approve it, export its cut list, then change kerf from 3 to 4 mm. The previous approval becomes invalid. The agent replans all 14 parts and ends at revision 2: staged, not approved . These are illustrative planning results—not measured workshop savings, machine instructions, or a safe-cutting guarantee. video_transcript_excerpt: Offcut gives people and browser agents the same cutting stock workbench. 14 parts fit. The long board stays protected. These illustrative measurements cover usable stock, parts, kerf, and the reusable remnant threshold. People own measurements and protection. Registered tools cannot change them. The right-hand panel is an external Mavo recording harness, not a chatbot inside the website. A real model chooses native WebM CP calls on the shared committed workbench. This is not a chat GPT recording. The model compares three complete alternatives, less stock, fewer boards, or useful offcuts. The deterministic branch-and-bound solver checks quantities, stock, and one kerf per part. A search limit is not proof of optimality. Less stock and fewer boards both open 7.2 m across three boards, 42 mm of sawdust plus 158 mm of short scrap. Keeping useful offcuts opens 10.08 m across six boards, 42 mm of sawdust, no short scrap, and 3.038 m reusable. Computed tradeoffs, not measured time or carbon savings. The agent inspects and stages the exact plan. Pause for review. This is not approval. Check stock identities, quantities, and kerf. No registered tool can approve. These UI controls are automated, not proof of human presence. Now, the controls check the acknowledgement. Then, they click approve cut sheet. The model inspects approval and exports the actual CSV. 14 parts, part identifiers, offsets, kerf, and the exact approved plan identifier. Another draft cannot inherit approval. Typing four leaves committed kerf at three. Pending at its block staging without moving focus or saving. Now commit. Revision two invalidates the old approval. The old plan is stale. The model replans 14 parts, 56 mm of sawdust. Revision two is staged, not approved. The acknowledgement stays unchecked. Offcut itself needs no account, model key or make end. The workbench and MIT licensed source are public. These are planning estimates, not machine instructions. Verify usable stock and safe cutting conditions at the bench.

live_observation.first_impression: Offcut opens directly into a populated cutting-plan workbench with stock, parts, kerf, and reusable-remnant settings.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked Find a cutting plan using the preloaded workshop measurements.
live_observation.after_state: The action did not return before the browser command timed out, so no plan result or approval state was verified.
live_observation.notes: The central workflow and separation between staging and approval were clearly exposed; WebMCP was labeled unavailable in manual mode.
